270.body:
**Asakusa View Hotel Annex Rokku**, operated by Hulic Hotel Management Co., Ltd., has been selected as a **"Selected Hotel"** in the "MICHELIN Guide Hotel Selection 2026" for the second year in a row, three years after opening in 2023.

The hotel was originally scheduled to open in 2020, but the opening was postponed due to the pandemic, and it opened in March 2023. It is located in "Asakusa Koen Rokku" (Asakusa Park Rokku), an area lined with movie theaters, yose (variety halls) and theaters since the early Showa era. Its concept is an experiential hotel where guests can feel the real Asakusa.

## Highlights That Earned Recognition

- **Stage events**: At the first-floor restaurant "Broadway Rokku," guests can enjoy performances of Asakusa geisha dance and Noh every weekend on a hinoki cypress stage relocated from the Kabuki-za Theatre in Ginza. Guests can also take commemorative photos with the performers. It is a restaurant theater where you can enjoy dishes made with a focus on dashi broth.
- **Japanese design**: While incorporating an Art Deco style, the entrance is designed to evoke a kabuki theater and uses wooden joinery made of Nara's Yoshino hinoki cypress. The guest rooms also feature kabuki elements and chabudai-style (low dining table-style) tables.
- **Premium lounge "FURUMAI"**: This lounge on the 10th floor is exclusively for hotel guests. Guests can enjoy famous Asakusa confections, old-fashioned sweets and drinks free of charge while taking in views of Tokyo Skytree®.
- **Breakfast**: The menu makes use of ingredients from long-established local Asakusa shops, including the Asakusa Burger and a Japanese set meal featuring Fukagawa-meshi. The Asakusa Burger is scheduled to be discontinued in April 2027.

"Selected" is a MICHELIN category for about 250 accommodations in Japan. The hotel was recognized for offering experiences unique to Asakusa.

273.title: Kamaasa Shoten x Tokyo Chainsaws Release "Tokyo Wood Cutting Board," Exclusively at the Kappabashi Store
273.summary: Kamaasa Shoten, a cookware specialty store in Kappabashi, has teamed up with Tokyo Chainsaws to release the "Tokyo Wood Cutting Board," made from a kaya (Japanese nutmeg yew) tree about 200 years old. It will go on sale exclusively at the Kappabashi store on October 13, 2026.
273.body:
## Bringing Tokyo Wood into the Kitchen

Kamaasa Shoten, a cookware specialty store in Kappabashi, has joined forces with Tokyo Chainsaws, a forestry company based in Hinohara Village, Tokyo, to launch a new initiative that delivers wood grown in Tokyo as cooking tools. As the first product, the "Tokyo Wood Cutting Board," made from a kaya (Japanese nutmeg yew) tree about 200 years old that stood at a shrine in Tokyo, will go on sale **exclusively at the Kamaasa Shoten Kappabashi store from October 13, 2026**.

## A Once-in-a-Lifetime Encounter with a Kaya Tree

The wood comes from a kaya tree that was the sacred tree of a shrine. A neighboring cedar was in danger of falling, and the kaya was to be cut down along with it when the cedar was felled. Tokyo Chainsaws inspected the logs on site and took them over because kaya is a rare species and the logs could yield straight-grained (masame) lumber suited to cutting boards. Tokyo Chainsaws handled the processing, and the finishing was done by a workshop that Kamaasa Shoten has long entrusted with making its cutting boards. Through "choshiage," a process of thinly shaving the surface, the boards have a smooth finish that brings out the beautiful grain of the kaya.

## Product Details

- Product name: Tokyo Wood Cutting Board – Kaya (Japanese nutmeg yew)
- Sizes and prices (tax included): Small 30 x 20 x 3 cm: 9,900 yen / Large 40 x 25 x 3 cm: 33,000 yen
- Available at: Exclusively at the Kamaasa Shoten Kappabashi store

## Features of Kaya Wood

Kaya has a moderate springiness and hardness, making it gentle on knife blades. Its fibers are supple, so cut marks are less likely to remain, and its natural oils give it antibacterial and water-resistant properties. Another appeal is its mild scent, which is unlikely to transfer to food.

The store is located at 2-24-1 Matsugaya, Taito-ku, Tokyo, and is open from 11:00 to 17:30 (open every day except the New Year holidays).

Sato, an ordinary person who had been a big fan of his since long ago, starts sharing a home with Kato and supports his daily life, hoping to help him get back on his feet. The shared life seemed to go well at first, but gradually fell apart, and in the end the two came to blows and parted ways.

Even though Kato's drinking was the cause, why did it escalate to the point of a fistfight? The story uncovers the reason by depicting Sato's family background.

284.body:
## A Base for Encountering Edo Culture Opens in Senzoku

Taito City is home to places associated with Tsutaya Juzaburo (Tsutajū), who supported Edo's publishing culture. Around Yoshiwara (now Senzoku), where Tsutajū was born, many historic sites remain, including the site of Koshodo, the Mikaeri Yanagi (Looking-Back Willow) and Yoshiwara Shrine. Now, "Edo Sui Koshodo" is opening as a base for exploring these sites.

## Facility Overview

- **Period**: Friday, October 16 – Sunday, December 6, 2026
- **Hours**: 11:00–16:00
- **Closed**: Every Monday (the following day if Monday is a national holiday)
- **Location**: Yoshiwara Kaikan (4-24-12 Senzoku, Taito-ku, Tokyo)
- **Admission**: Free (no merchandise sales)

From Asakusa, take the Toei Bus Kusa 64 from "Tobu Asakusa Station" and get off at "Yoshiwara Odamon," then walk 6 minutes. The trip takes about 15 minutes.

## Exhibition

Works related to Tsutajū are on display, including *Yoshiwara Saiken* and *Seiro Bijin Awase Sugata Kagami*. Many original prints made at the time are also on view. Noren curtains and andon lanterns used in the filming of the NHK Taiga drama "Berabo: Tsutajū Eiga no Yumebanashi" are also exhibited.

## Stamp Rally and Events

A stamp rally will be held in which you visit five stamp points and stamp overlapping impressions on a stamp card to complete an ukiyo-e print. The completed card can be used as a postcard.

Free events include guided walking tours, ozashiki dance by Shimabara Tayu, rakugo by Katsura Mikisuke, a terakoya (Edo-period school) experience and an ukiyo-e printing experience. Events require advance registration, and a lottery will be held if applications exceed capacity. Details are subject to change.
